Edda Voss had kept the light at Marrow Point for thirty-one years, and in all that time she had never once seen the beam she tended. This was not a figure of speech. The lamp sat two hundred feet above her, at the top of a spiral stair she no longer trusted her knees to climb, and its light fell outward across the water, away from the tower, away from her. She knew its color only from photographs taken by passing boats — a white so pure it looked blue in the dark, cutting the horizon into even slices, five seconds of light, five seconds of nothing, forever.

Her grandson Teo climbed the stairs for her now. He was nineteen and impatient with the mechanism, which was older than the two of them combined and did not care. Twice a night he wound the clockwork that turned the lens, checked the oil reservoir, wiped the glass with a chamois cloth that had belonged to his great-grandfather. He came down each time smelling of kerosene and cold air, and each time he said some version of the same thing: this is absurd, there are satellites now, there are apps that tell you where the rocks are, nobody needs this anymore.

Edda let him say it. She had said it herself once, to her own grandmother, who had kept the light before her and had answered only by handing her a rag and pointing up the stairs.

"Someone needs it," Edda said instead, "or the harbor master wouldn't pay for the oil."

"The harbor master is seventy years old and sentimental."

"So are you going to be, someday, if you're lucky."

Teo laughed, but he went back up the stairs anyway, because that was the arrangement. She managed the logbook and the radio and the small grey cottage at the tower's base; he managed his knees, which worked, in exchange for hers, which did not.

The logbook was the part of the work Edda loved best, though she would not have called it love if anyone asked. It was a ledger, bound in oilcloth, and in it she recorded the weather, the ships that passed, the small emergencies — a flare seen at 2 a.m. that turned out to be a bonfire on the mainland, a fishing boat that lost its engine in a chop and had to be towed in by the Coast Guard while she radioed its position every ten minutes until it was safe. Entries went back generations. She had read them all, on slow nights, in the years before Teo came to live with her. She knew the hand of every keeper of Marrow Point going back to 1888, when the tower was built on a rock that had already swallowed eleven ships, and the government had finally decided that was eleven too many.

The log for 1931 was her favorite. A keeper named Absalom Pruitt had written, in a cramped and furious hand, about a storm that had torn the roof from the oil shed and nearly taken the tower's door off its hinges, and in the middle of recounting the wind speeds and the barometric pressure, he had simply written: I do not know why I am afraid of dying here when I have spent my whole life making sure other people don't. Then, the next line, matter-of-fact again: Oil reserves sufficient through March.

She thought about that line often. I do not know why I am afraid of dying here when I have spent my whole life making sure other people don't. She had never written anything like it in her own entries, which were plain and procedural, because she did not think the log was the place for such things, but she understood the impulse. There was something about the tower at night — the particular quality of the silence between the foghorn's blasts, the way the light swept overhead and never touched you — that made a person feel both enormously important and completely irrelevant, sometimes within the same hour.

Teo did not feel this yet. He felt only the cold and the repetition and the fact that none of his friends on the mainland had to climb two hundred and forty-one steps twice a night to keep a nineteenth-century lamp burning. He had come to Marrow Point the autumn after his mother died, not because anyone forced him, but because there had been nowhere else that made sense, and Edda had not asked questions, only put him to work, which he was later, much later, going to tell people was the kindest thing anyone had done for him that year. Work with a shape to it. Work that could not be postponed by grief, because the light did not care whether you were grieving. The light needed oil at six and midnight regardless.

It was in the second winter that the storm came that mattered — not the kind that tore the roof off a shed, but the kind that takes a whole boat. A trawler called the Agnes May had gone out past the point against every forecast, chasing a run of fish that the captain swore was worth the risk, and the risk had turned out to be a nor'easter that built itself out of nothing in four hours. Edda heard the mayday on the radio at 9:40 p.m., a man's voice gone thin with cold and fear, giving a position that put him somewhere inside the worst stretch of water Marrow Point watched over, a reef shelf the charts called the Combs because of what it did to hulls.

She sent Teo up the stairs before he had his coat properly on. "Full power," she said. "Check the lens is clean, check the mechanism is turning true, and then get back down here and get on the radio with me, because I will need two voices." He did not ask why two voices. He went.

The Coast Guard cutter was forty minutes out, which in that water, in that wind, might as well have been a geological age. Edda stayed on the radio with the Agnes May's captain, a man named Delacroix who kept apologizing between bursts of static, as if the storm were a personal failing, and she told him the same thing over and over in a voice she had trained over three decades not to let shake: hold your position relative to the light, don't try to outrun the reef, let the light tell you where you are and trust it, because the light does not move and your instincts right now will lie to you.

Teo came down from the tower white-faced and breathing hard and sat by the radio and did not speak, only listened, because she had told him that was the job right now — to be another ear, another set of eyes on the chart, nothing more. Twice he started to say something and twice she held up a hand, not unkindly, and he swallowed it.

At 11:06 p.m. Delacroix's voice cracked through, not with fear this time but with something close to wonder. I see it. I see the light. We're turning. And then, twenty unbearable minutes later, the cutter's radio confirming a position, a line thrown, four men and one very lucky dog pulled off a boat that went down against the Combs eleven minutes after the last man left its deck.

Afterward, Teo sat on the cottage steps with a blanket around his shoulders that he did not remember anyone giving him, and Edda sat beside him with two cups of coffee neither of them drank, and the light kept turning overhead, five seconds on, five seconds off, indifferent and essential, the way it had turned every night since 1888 and would turn every night after both of them were gone, if someone kept climbing the stairs.

"You asked me once why anyone needs this," Edda said, "when there are satellites."

"I remember."

"Satellites don't climb two hundred steps in a gale to check that the lens is clean. Satellites don't stand here and listen to a man's voice shaking and tell him to trust something bigger than his own fear. The light is a machine. What it does isn't." She looked at him, and in the dark she could not see his face clearly, only its shape, and that was enough. "That's the part of the job that isn't in the logbook. I'm telling you now so it's written down somewhere."

Teo was quiet for a long moment, and then he said, in a voice much younger than nineteen, "I still think the knees are the worse end of the deal."
